title: Maximum depth of a binary tree → minimum depth
label: single
statement: Return the **maximum depth** of a binary tree: the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf. An empty tree has depth 0.
provenance: Reported in a LinkedIn **elimination round** (your recent list, Oct 2026), paired with Zigzag Level Order. LeetCode 104; the follow-up is LeetCode 111.

sources.name: Your list of recently asked LinkedIn coding questions (supplied 26 Oct 2026)

clarify: Depth in nodes or edges? (Nodes — a single node is 1.)
How deep can it be? (Very — assume a 100,000-node chain, so plain recursion may overflow.)

stages.title: Maximum depth
stages.say: Return the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path.
stages.require: Implement `TreeDepth.Max(root)`. Empty → 0. Must survive a 100,000-deep tree.

stages.title: Minimum depth
stages.say: Now return the depth of the nearest leaf.
stages.require: Add `TreeDepth.Min(root)`: nodes on the shortest root-to-leaf path. A node with one child is not a leaf.
testNames: a missing child is not a leaf
a shallow leaf beside a 100,000-deep chain

1.a: Ask. LeetCode counts nodes; some interviewers count edges (one less).

2.a: O(n) time; O(width) memory for BFS, O(h) for DFS.
Three lines: 1 + max(left, right). Say it overflows on a deep chain, and offer BFS.

4.q: Minimum depth on a huge tree.
4.a: BFS wins: it stops at the first leaf; DFS must visit everything.

5.a: Empty, single node, lopsided, a deep chain, and a shallow leaf next to a deep branch.

prompts.label: Check my design — no code
prompts.text: I believe walk the tree level by level with a queue and count the levels; the minimum depth is the level of the first leaf BFS meets — O(n), and no recursion, so a 100,000-deep tree is fine. Review my reasoning without giving me the implementation. What would break it?

prompts.label: Review, do not rewrite
prompts.text: Review my implementation for correctness and edge cases. Do not rewrite the code. List problems most severe first, each with the input that triggers it.

prompts.label: Race conditions
prompts.text: Now review this implementation for race conditions if multiple threads call Max concurrently. For each race, give the interleaving that breaks it. Then name the smallest synchronization boundary that preserves correctness. Do not write code yet.

prompts.label: Tests that expose bugs
prompts.text: Suggest tests that could expose bugs in my implementation: boundaries, duplicates, empty and invalid input, and concurrency where it applies. For each, say why the expected value is correct.

prompts.label: Complexity check
prompts.text: What is the time and space complexity of each public method as written? Do not claim a bound unless every step achieves it.

prompts.label: Requirement change
prompts.text: The requirement changed: Add TreeDepth.Min(root): nodes on the shortest root-to-leaf path. A node with one child is not a leaf. List which members need to change and which do not, before writing any code.

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md: Return the **maximum depth** of a binary tree: the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf. An empty tree has depth 0.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
- Depth in nodes or edges? (Nodes — a single node is 1.)
- Empty tree? (0.)
- How deep can it be? (Very — assume a 100,000-node chain, so plain recursion may overflow.)

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md: Depth is just "how many levels are there". BFS processes one whole level per loop, so counting loops gives the depth — and it never recurses.

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md:
- Recursion on a 100,000-deep chain → StackOverflowException, which crashes the process.
- Counting edges instead of nodes.
- For minimum depth: taking min(left, right) when one child is missing — a missing child is not a leaf.
